overview: SCD Type 1 (Slowly Changing Dimension Type 1) is a strategy for handling changes to dimension attributes by overwriting the old value with the new value, keeping no history of the prior state.
After a Type 1 update, the dimension reflects only the current truth; all historical facts effectively appear as if the attribute always had its current value.
It is the simplest SCD strategy, implemented with an UPDATE or MERGE/UPSERT, and is appropriate when history does not matter or when correcting data errors.
learningObjectives: Understand how SCD Type 1 overwrites attribute values and discards history.
Recognize when Type 1 is acceptable (corrections, non-historical attributes) versus when Type 2 is required.
Implement SCD Type 1 with a MERGE/UPSERT and reason about its trade-offs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: SCD Type 1 is a dimension-change handling technique in which an updated source attribute overwrites the existing dimension value in place, retaining no record of the previous value. The dimension row keeps its surrogate key, and no new version is created, so the change is reflected uniformly across all historical and current fact rows that reference that dimension row.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine an address book where, when a friend moves, you erase the old address and write the new one over it. You now know where they live today, but you have no record of where they used to live. That is SCD Type 1: overwrite and forget the past.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Slowly Changing Dimensions were categorized by Ralph Kimball in dimensional modeling literature, with Types 1, 2, and 3 as the foundational strategies (later extended to Types 0, 4, 5, 6/7). Type 1 represents the original 'just overwrite' approach used before history-tracking requirements led to Type 2.

whyItMatters.business: Type 1 keeps dimensions showing the current, correct value, which is exactly what the business wants for attributes like a corrected spelling, a current phone number, or a fixed data-entry error.
whyItMatters.engineering: It is the cheapest SCD to build and maintain: a simple overwrite via UPDATE/MERGE with no version management, effective-date columns, or row explosion.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because no new rows are created on change, the dimension stays compact and fact joins remain simple and fast, unlike the version growth of Type 2.
whyItMatters.cost: Minimal storage and ETL cost; no proliferation of historical versions to store, index, or scan.
whyItMatters.reliability: Straightforward logic reduces the chance of bugs, but choosing Type 1 where history is actually needed silently destroys auditability, so the strategy choice must be deliberate.

coreComponents.name: Surrogate Key (Stable)
coreComponents.definition: The dimension's primary key, which does not change during a Type 1 update.
coreComponents.purpose: To keep all referencing facts pointing to the same row even as its attributes are overwritten.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Remains constant; only descriptive attributes change in place.
coreComponents.examples: customer_key = 8821 stays the same when the customer's email is corrected

coreComponents.name: Natural (Business) Key
coreComponents.definition: The source identifier used to match an incoming source row to the existing dimension row.
coreComponents.purpose: To determine whether an incoming record is a new entity (insert) or an existing one (overwrite).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Drives the MERGE/UPSERT match condition between staging and the dimension.
coreComponents.examples: customer_id from the CRM used in the MERGE ON clause

coreComponents.name: Overwritable Attributes
coreComponents.definition: The descriptive columns updated in place when the source value changes.
coreComponents.purpose: To hold only the current value of each attribute, discarding prior values.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Are replaced by the new source value during the update; no prior value is retained.

internalWorking: The ETL stages incoming source rows and matches each to the dimension on the natural/business key.
If no matching dimension row exists, a new row is inserted with a freshly generated surrogate key (the INSERT branch).

If a matching row exists and any tracked attribute differs, the existing row's attributes are overwritten with the new values in place, keeping the same surrogate key (the UPDATE branch); the previous values are lost.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source Change -> Staging -> MERGE on natural key: (no match) INSERT new row | (match + changed attrs) UPDATE/overwrite in place -> Dimension reflects only current values -> Facts unchanged (same surrogate key)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. dim_customer holds customer_key=8821, customer_id='C-552', email='old@x.com', city='Austin'.
2. The CRM sends an updated record: customer_id='C-552', email='new@x.com', city='Austin'.
3. MERGE matches on customer_id='C-552'; email differs, so the row is updated in place to email='new@x.com', keeping customer_key=8821.
4. Every existing and future fact referencing customer_key=8821 now joins to email='new@x.com'; the old email is gone with no history.

keyTerminology.meaning: Replacing the existing attribute value with the new value on the same row, discarding the old value.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines the essence of Type 1 and distinguishes it from history-preserving strategies.

keyTerminology.meaning: A single statement that inserts new rows when there is no match and updates existing rows when there is a match.
keyTerminology.importance: The standard, atomic way to implement Type 1 (and other SCD inserts) in modern SQL engines.

keyTerminology.meaning: A strategy that preserves history by inserting a new versioned row (with effective dates and a current flag) instead of overwriting.
keyTerminology.importance: The primary alternative to Type 1; chosen when historical accuracy of attributes is required.

keyTerminology.meaning: A strategy where the attribute is never changed after initial load (retain original).
keyTerminology.importance: Contrasts with Type 1's overwrite; used for fixed attributes like original signup date.

importantConcepts.explanation: Type 1 is appropriate when the prior value has no analytical or audit value: correcting data-entry errors (misspelled names), updating cosmetic/descriptive attributes, or attributes the business explicitly wants to always reflect current state. It is the right choice when 'as-is' reporting (current value applied to all history) is desired.

Because the overwrite changes how all existing facts join to the dimension, prior reports can change when re-run. A customer who was in the 'West' region last year will appear to have always been in their new region. This restatement is acceptable for corrections but dangerous for attributes where point-in-time accuracy matters (use Type 2 then).

variationsAndTypes: **Pure Type 1 (overwrite):** Replace the attribute, keep no trace of the old value.
**Type 1 with audit columns:** Overwrite the business attribute but update last_updated / updated_by metadata for operational traceability (still no business history).
**Hybrid (Type 1 + Type 2 attributes):** In the same dimension, some attributes are Type 1 (overwrite) and others are Type 2 (versioned), chosen per attribute based on whether history matters.
advantages: **Simplicity:** Easiest SCD to implement and reason about — a single overwrite.
**Compact Dimension:** No new rows on change, so the dimension stays small and joins stay fast.
**Current Truth Always:** Reports always reflect the latest, corrected attribute value.
**Low Cost:** Minimal storage and ETL overhead with no version management.
disadvantages: **No History:** The previous value is permanently lost; you cannot do point-in-time analysis.
**History Restatement:** Re-running old reports can yield different results because the dimension changed under them.
**Audit Gaps:** Unsuitable where regulatory or analytical auditability of changes is required.
**Irreversible:** Once overwritten, the old value cannot be recovered without a separate backup or change log.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use Type 1 for correcting errors, for purely descriptive/cosmetic attributes, or when the business explicitly wants current values applied retroactively to all facts (no need to preserve prior states).
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid Type 1 when history matters: when you must analyze facts against the attribute value that was true at the time of the event, or when auditing/compliance requires a record of what changed and when (use Type 2).

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: SCD Type 1 is like updating a contact's photo in your phone: the new photo replaces the old one and you no longer have the previous picture. You always see them as they look now, with no album of how they looked before.

commonMisconceptions.myth: SCD Type 1 keeps at least some history of changes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type 1 keeps no business history at all; the old value is overwritten and lost. If you need history, that is Type 2 (new versioned rows) or Type 3 (a 'previous value' column).

commonMisconceptions.myth: SCD Type 1 is harmless because it just fixes data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type 1 silently restates history: re-running prior reports can change because all facts now join to the new value. It is only safe when point-in-time accuracy of that attribute genuinely does not matter.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Type 1 scales well because updates do not grow the dimension. The main cost is the in-place UPDATE; on columnar/append-oriented engines, large overwrites can be expensive and may favor MERGE with partition rewrites.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make the load idempotent: a MERGE keyed on the natural key produces the same result whether run once or many times, and only updates rows whose attributes actually changed.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Wrap the MERGE in a transaction so a failed batch leaves the dimension consistent; on re-run, unchanged rows are skipped and changed rows reach the correct final state.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track the number of rows updated per load; an unusually high overwrite count can signal upstream data issues or a misclassified attribute that should be Type 2.
productionConsiderations.security: Overwriting can erase data needed for audits; ensure any compliance-sensitive attribute is not Type 1, or keep a separate change-data-capture log if traceability is required.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Only update rows where a tracked attribute changed (compare hashes or use a WHEN MATCHED AND condition) to avoid rewriting unchanged rows and incurring needless I/O.
productionConsiderations.performance: Match on an indexed natural key and update only changed rows; on engines that dislike updates, consider MERGE that rewrites affected partitions efficiently.

codeExamples.title: SCD Type 1 via MERGE (Overwrite on Change)
codeExamples.overview: A standard MERGE/UPSERT that inserts new customers and overwrites changed attributes in place, only updating rows that actually changed.
codeExamples.code:
MERGE INTO dim_customer AS tgt
USING staging_customer AS src
   ON tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id        -- match on natural/business key
WHEN MATCHED
     AND (tgt.email <> src.email
          OR tgt.phone <> src.phone
          OR tgt.city  <> src.city)            -- only update if something changed
THEN UPDATE SET
     tgt.email        = src.email,             -- overwrite in place (no history)
     tgt.phone        = src.phone,
     tgt.city         = src.city,
     tgt.last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
     INSERT (customer_id, email, phone, city, last_updated)
     VALUES (src.customer_id, src.email, src.phone, src.city, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP);
codeExamples.breakdown: The MERGE matches staging to the dimension on the natural key customer_id. WHEN MATCHED with the change condition overwrites email/phone/city in place (the surrogate key is untouched, so facts are unaffected). WHEN NOT MATCHED inserts a brand-new customer row. The previous values are discarded.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: New customers are inserted; existing customers with changed attributes have those attributes overwritten; unchanged rows are skipped. No historical versions are created.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Omitting the change condition rewrites every matched row each run, wasting I/O. Using NULL-unsafe comparisons (<>) can skip changes where one side is NULL; use IS DISTINCT FROM (or COALESCE) for null-safe comparison.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Compare a hash of the tracked attributes (e.g., MD5 of concatenated columns) in the WHEN MATCHED clause to detect changes efficiently across many columns.

codeExamples.title: SCD Type 1 via Plain UPDATE (Single-Source Correction)
codeExamples.overview: When you simply need to correct values for existing rows, a targeted UPDATE overwrites them in place.
codeExamples.code:
-- Correct a misspelled product name across the dimension (Type 1 overwrite)
UPDATE dim_product
SET    product_name = 'Organic Bananas',
       last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE  product_sku = 'A-100'
  AND  product_name <> 'Organic Bananas';
codeExamples.breakdown: This overwrites product_name for the matching SKU in place, keeping the same surrogate product_key so all facts immediately reflect the corrected name. The trailing predicate avoids touching rows that already hold the correct value.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The product name is corrected on the existing dimension row; every fact referencing it now shows the corrected name, with no record of the misspelling retained.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Updating without the inequality predicate touches rows needlessly. Forgetting that this restates history means old reports will now show the corrected name even for past periods.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Index product_sku for fast lookup; for bulk corrections, batch updates by partition to limit lock scope and rewrite cost.

codeExamples.title: Null-Safe Change Detection for Robust Type 1
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates IS DISTINCT FROM so that changes involving NULLs are still detected and overwritten.
codeExamples.code:
MERGE INTO dim_customer AS tgt
USING staging_customer AS src
   ON tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED
     AND (tgt.email IS DISTINCT FROM src.email
          OR tgt.phone IS DISTINCT FROM src.phone
          OR tgt.marital_status IS DISTINCT FROM src.marital_status)
THEN UPDATE SET
     tgt.email          = src.email,
     tgt.phone          = src.phone,
     tgt.marital_status = src.marital_status,
     tgt.last_updated   = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;
codeExamples.breakdown: IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value, so a change from NULL to a real value (or vice versa) is correctly detected, unlike <> which returns UNKNOWN when either side is NULL. This prevents missed Type 1 overwrites.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Rows are overwritten whenever any tracked attribute genuinely changed, including transitions to or from NULL; truly unchanged rows are skipped.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Engines lacking IS DISTINCT FROM (some older SQL dialects) require COALESCE-based comparisons or null-handling logic to achieve the same result.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: On engines without IS DISTINCT FROM, use COALESCE(col, sentinel) <> COALESCE(src.col, sentinel) with a sentinel value that cannot occur in the data.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription company maintains a customer dimension where contact details and a few descriptive attributes frequently get corrected. The business wants reports to always show current, corrected contact info and does not need to analyze historical contact values.
endToEndExample.inputData: Daily CRM extract of customers (customer_id, email, phone, city, marital_status) staged into staging_customer.
endToEndExample.architecture: A star schema with dim_customer (surrogate customer_key, natural customer_id, descriptive attributes, last_updated) referenced by fact_subscription_events. Contact attributes are designated SCD Type 1.
processingSteps: 1. Land the daily CRM extract into staging_customer.
2. Run a MERGE matching on customer_id.
3. WHEN NOT MATCHED, insert new customers with a new surrogate key.
4. WHEN MATCHED and tracked attributes changed (null-safe), overwrite email/phone/city/marital_status in place and set last_updated.
5. Load facts referencing the stable customer_key; no fact changes are needed for Type 1 updates.
endToEndExample.output: A dim_customer that always reflects current contact details, with the same surrogate keys preserved so existing facts continue to join correctly, now showing the latest values.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track rows inserted vs overwritten per run; alert if the overwrite volume spikes (possible upstream data corruption) or if an attribute intended to be historical is being overwritten.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The MERGE runs in a transaction and is idempotent: a re-run after failure only overwrites rows that still differ and inserts only genuinely new customers, so no duplicates or partial states remain.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Clean, current customer attributes with minimal ETL cost. The trade-off is accepted explicitly: no history of prior contact details is kept, which is fine for these corrective/cosmetic attributes; any attribute needing history would instead be modeled as SCD Type 2.

industryUseCases.problem: Customer contact details and cosmetic profile attributes are frequently corrected and should always show current values.
industryUseCases.solution: Model email, phone, and display name as SCD Type 1 attributes, overwriting them in place via MERGE.
industryUseCases.benefits: Simple, low-cost dimension maintenance with reports always reflecting current, corrected contact info.

industryUseCases.problem: Product master data contains data-entry errors (misspelled names, wrong descriptions) that must be fixed everywhere.
industryUseCases.solution: Apply Type 1 overwrites to descriptive product attributes so corrections propagate to all facts referencing the product.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, corrected product labeling across all historical and current reporting without version bloat.

industryUseCases.company: Healthcare Operations (non-clinical, e.g., hospital admin systems)
industryUseCases.problem: Administrative attributes like a patient's preferred contact phone or mailing address change and only the current value is needed operationally.
industryUseCases.solution: Use Type 1 for these operational attributes while keeping clinically significant or audited attributes as Type 2.
industryUseCases.benefits: Current operational data is always accurate, while compliance-sensitive attributes retain history under a different SCD strategy.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Type 1 does not grow the dimension on change, keeping it compact and joins fast. The cost is the in-place UPDATE; on columnar/lakehouse engines, prefer MERGE that rewrites only affected partitions and update only changed rows.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Implement the load as an idempotent MERGE in a transaction so a retried batch reaches the same final state without duplicates or partial overwrites.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Dimensions are read-heavy; schedule Type 1 overwrites in short transactions to minimize lock contention, and replicate dimensions so analytical reads stay available during refreshes.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because Type 1 destroys prior values, rely on source master data and time-travel/snapshots to recover from an erroneous overwrite; consider a CDC/change log if any traceability is needed.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Match on an indexed natural key, detect changes with hashes or IS DISTINCT FROM, and update only rows that changed to avoid rewriting unchanged data.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Skip rewriting unchanged rows and avoid versioning overhead; Type 1 is the cheapest SCD when history is genuinely unnecessary.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Ensure compliance-sensitive attributes are not modeled as Type 1, since overwriting erases the audit trail; keep a separate change log where regulation requires it.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track insert vs update counts and the set of attributes overwritten; spikes can indicate upstream corruption or an attribute misclassified as Type 1 instead of Type 2.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that the MERGE match on natural key is unique, that change detection is null-safe, and that the load is idempotent across re-runs.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log each overwrite (optionally to an audit/CDC table) and alert on abnormal overwrite volumes or overwrites of attributes flagged as historical.

recommendedPractices: **Choose Type 1 deliberately per attribute:** Use it only where prior values have no analytical or audit value.
**Implement with an idempotent MERGE:** Match on the natural key and overwrite only when tracked attributes actually changed.
**Use null-safe change detection:** Prefer IS DISTINCT FROM (or COALESCE comparisons) so NULL transitions are caught.
**Keep the surrogate key stable:** Overwrite attributes in place without changing the key so facts remain correctly joined.
engineeringStandards: Document each dimension attribute's SCD type (0/1/2/3) and the rationale.
Type 1 loads must be idempotent and run within a transaction.
Only rows with genuine attribute changes are updated; unchanged rows are skipped.
designRecommendations: Use Type 1 for corrections and cosmetic/descriptive attributes; use Type 2 for attributes needing point-in-time history.
Consider hybrid dimensions where some attributes are Type 1 and others Type 2.
Maintain a last_updated (and optionally updated_by) column for operational traceability even though business history is not kept.
If any change traceability is required, pair Type 1 with a separate CDC/change-log table.
namingConventions: Prefix dimensions with `dim_` and keep the surrogate key as `<entity>_key`.
Name the audit metadata column consistently (e.g., last_updated, updated_by).
Flag the SCD type in the data dictionary (e.g., scd_type = 1) per attribute.
documentationStandards: Record which attributes are Type 1 and explicitly note that history is not preserved.
Document the MERGE match key and change-detection logic.
Explain the business decision to accept history restatement for each Type 1 attribute.
testingStrategies: Test that a changed attribute is overwritten and the surrogate key is unchanged.
Test idempotency by running the MERGE twice and confirming no duplicate inserts and stable final values.
Test null-safe change detection (NULL -> value and value -> NULL).
Test that unchanged rows are not rewritten (verify update count is zero when nothing changed).

commonMistakes.mistake: Using Type 1 for an attribute that needs history.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Type 1 is the default/easiest choice and the history requirement is overlooked.
commonMistakes.impact: Point-in-time analysis becomes impossible and prior reports silently change; audit trails are destroyed.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Classify each attribute: use Type 2 (versioned rows) where the value-at-event-time matters; reserve Type 1 for corrections and non-historical attributes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overwriting every matched row regardless of whether it changed.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Writing the MERGE without a WHEN MATCHED AND change condition.
commonMistakes.impact: Needless I/O and rewrites on every load, hurting performance and inflating last_updated noise.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add a null-safe change condition (IS DISTINCT FROM or hash comparison) so only genuinely changed rows are overwritten.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using NULL-unsafe comparisons for change detection.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using <> which returns UNKNOWN (treated as false) when either operand is NULL.
commonMistakes.impact: Changes to or from NULL are missed, so the dimension silently retains stale values.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use IS DISTINCT FROM or COALESCE-based comparisons to make change detection null-safe.

comparisonSection.explanation: Type 1 overwrites the attribute in place and keeps no history, so all facts reflect the current value. Type 2 inserts a new row (new surrogate key) with effective/expiry dates and a current flag, preserving the value that was true at the time of each fact for accurate point-in-time analysis.

Type 1 is the simplest and cheapest (a single in-place update, compact dimension). Type 2 adds version management, effective dating, current flags, and row growth, increasing ETL and storage cost. Type 3 adds a limited 'previous value' column, preserving only one prior value.

Under Type 1 the surrogate key is unchanged, so existing facts automatically reflect the new value (history restated). Under Type 2 existing facts keep pointing to the old version's surrogate key, so they retain the historical value, while new facts reference the new current version.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is SCD Type 1?
beginnerQuestions.answer: SCD Type 1 handles changes to a dimension attribute by overwriting the old value with the new value in place, keeping no history. The dimension always shows the current value, and the surrogate key stays the same.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize overwrite-and-forget and that no historical version is created.

beginnerQuestions.question: When is SCD Type 1 acceptable?
beginnerQuestions.answer: When the previous value has no analytical or audit value, such as correcting data-entry errors, updating cosmetic/descriptive attributes, or when the business wants the current value applied to all history.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Contrast with cases where history matters, which require Type 2.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you implement SCD Type 1, and why use MERGE?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use a MERGE/UPSERT keyed on the natural/business key: WHEN NOT MATCHED inserts a new row, and WHEN MATCHED AND attributes changed overwrites them in place. MERGE handles insert and update atomically in one idempotent statement, and the change condition avoids rewriting unchanged rows.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention null-safe change detection (IS DISTINCT FROM) and keeping the surrogate key stable so facts are unaffected.

intermediateQuestions.question: What are the trade-offs of SCD Type 1 versus Type 2?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Type 1 is simple, compact, and cheap but loses history and restates prior reports. Type 2 preserves point-in-time history with versioned rows and effective dates but adds ETL/storage complexity and row growth. Choose Type 1 for corrections/non-historical attributes and Type 2 when value-at-event-time matters.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Frame it as a simplicity/cost vs historical-accuracy trade-off; mention hybrid dimensions mixing both per attribute.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can an SCD Type 1 update silently change the results of previously run reports, and how do you mitigate it?
advancedQuestions.answer: Because Type 1 overwrites the attribute on the same surrogate key, every fact referencing that row now joins to the new value, so re-running an old report restates history. Mitigation: only apply Type 1 to attributes where this is acceptable; for attributes needing point-in-time accuracy use Type 2; optionally keep a CDC/change log for traceability and snapshot reports if reproducibility is required.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates understanding of the restatement risk and the deliberate strategy choice between Type 1 and Type 2.

advancedQuestions.question: On a columnar/lakehouse engine that dislikes in-place updates, how do you implement Type 1 efficiently?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use a MERGE that rewrites only the affected partitions/files (e.g., Delta/Iceberg MERGE), detect changes with a hash or IS DISTINCT FROM so only genuinely changed rows are touched, and partition the dimension to bound the rewrite scope. This achieves the overwrite semantics while minimizing the cost of immutable storage.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows awareness that 'overwrite' on modern lakehouse engines is implemented as targeted file/partition rewrites via MERGE.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your dim_customer stores email, phone, and home_region. Marketing analyzes campaign response by the region a customer was in at the time of the campaign. A customer corrects a typo in their email and also genuinely relocates regions. How do you model these attributes?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Email and phone corrections have no analytical history value, so they are Type 1 (overwrite). home_region must reflect the value at the time of each campaign for accurate response analysis, so it requires point-in-time history and must be Type 2 (versioned). This yields a hybrid dimension.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Model email and phone as Type 1 (overwrite in place via MERGE). Model home_region as Type 2: when it changes, expire the current row and insert a new versioned row with a new surrogate key and effective dates, so historical facts keep the old region and new facts use the new one.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the dimension-update strategy for a customer dimension feeding both operational dashboards (current contact info) and longitudinal analytics (behavior by attributes at event time).
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use a hybrid SCD dimension. Operational/cosmetic attributes (email, phone, display name) are Type 1, overwritten via an idempotent MERGE on the natural key with null-safe change detection. Analytically time-sensitive attributes (segment, region, plan tier) are Type 2 with effective_date, expiry_date, and is_current. Facts reference the surrogate key, so Type 1 changes are transparent and Type 2 changes create new versions.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Type 1 attributes keep the dimension compact and reports current but lose history and restate prior dashboards; Type 2 attributes preserve point-in-time accuracy at the cost of row growth and ETL complexity. The hybrid balances cost against analytical need per attribute.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Index the natural key for MERGE matching; detect changes via column hashes; partition the dimension and rewrite only affected partitions on lakehouse engines. Cache the dimension in the semantic layer and run updates in short transactions to limit lock contention.

Why is IS DISTINCT FROM preferred over <> for change detection?
Can a single dimension mix Type 1 and Type 2 attributes? How?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: SCD Type 1 overwrites a dimension attribute in place with the new value, keeping no history of the prior value.
keyConcepts: Surrogate key stays stable; facts are unaffected.
Implemented with MERGE/UPSERT on the natural key.
Restates history; use Type 2 when point-in-time accuracy is needed.
formulas: N/A — SCD Type 1 is a procedural/structural pattern, not a formula.
Change-detection (null-safe): update WHEN tgt.col IS DISTINCT FROM src.col.
Idempotency: MERGE(run once) result == MERGE(run N times).
commands: MERGE INTO dim_customer t USING staging s ON t.customer_id=s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED AND t.email IS DISTINCT FROM s.email THEN UPDATE SET t.email=s.email WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);
UPDATE dim_product SET product_name='Organic Bananas' WHERE product_sku='A-100' AND product_name<>'Organic Bananas';
interviewPoints: Type 1 = overwrite, no history; Type 2 = versioned rows with history.
Surrogate key unchanged, so all facts reflect the new value (history restated).
Implement with an idempotent MERGE; only update changed rows.
Use null-safe change detection (IS DISTINCT FROM).
Choose per attribute; hybrid dimensions mix Type 1 and Type 2.
quickNotes: Type 1 keeps zero business history; the old value is gone forever.
Best for correcting errors and cosmetic/descriptive attributes.
MERGE matched-and-changed branch overwrites; not-matched branch inserts.
Re-running old reports can change because the dimension was overwritten.
On lakehouse engines, 'overwrite' = MERGE that rewrites affected partitions.

keyTakeaways: SCD Type 1 handles dimension changes by overwriting the old value in place and keeping no history, so the dimension always shows the current value and the surrogate key never changes.

It is the simplest, cheapest SCD strategy, implemented with an idempotent MERGE/UPSERT on the natural key that inserts new rows and overwrites only genuinely changed attributes (use null-safe change detection).

Because the surrogate key is stable, a Type 1 overwrite restates history: all existing facts now reflect the new value, which is why it suits corrections and non-historical attributes but not point-in-time analysis.

Choose Type 2 (versioned rows with effective dates) instead when the value at the time of each event matters or auditability is required; many dimensions are hybrids with Type 1 and Type 2 attributes side by side.
Type 1's trade-off is simplicity and compactness in exchange for permanently losing prior values, so the strategy must be chosen deliberately per attribute and documented.
